section_summary: This section consists chiefly of Peruvian press clippings from October 1937 debating Japanese immigration, landholding, employment, small business, and colonization. Most articles express strongly anti-Japanese and often explicitly racist fears about economic displacement, demographic change, espionage, and national sovereignty, while H. Ikeyama defends the Japanese community’s commercial and agricultural activities. Other pieces discuss immigration enforcement at Callao and the Perú Takushoku Kumiai agricultural settlement in Chanchamayo.

subfiles.title: La Inmigración Asiática y el Mejoramiento de la Raza
subfiles.about: An explicitly racialist argument for restricting Asian immigration while encouraging selected European and North American settlement in Peru.
subfiles.summary: Olivares links ancient American civilizations to Asian migration but depicts modern Asian immigration as threatening Peru's racial composition, economy and sovereignty, advocating European colonization.

subfiles.title: La Infiltración Japonesa: La Colonia Japonesa—El Pequeño Comercio y la Pequeña Industria IV
subfiles.doc_type: Newspaper clipping; Enclosure No. 37 to despatch No. 245
subfiles.about: An analysis of Japanese participation in Peru’s small businesses and trades and of governmental measures limiting foreign economic activity.
subfiles.summary: Article: Japanese migrants moved from farming to cafes, bakeries and barbering, sometimes displacing Chinese as well as Peruvians; cites license data and the June 26, 1936 decree, arguing legal restriction is needed.

subfiles.title: La Infiltración Japonesa
subfiles.doc_type: Newspaper clipping; Enclosure No. 38 to despatch No. 245
subfiles.from: Jorge Badani, President of the Asociación Rural del Perú
subfiles.about: An argument that high rents and superior Japanese cooperative credit were transferring coastal farmland from Peruvian to Japanese cultivators.
subfiles.summary: Badani attributes Japanese farm expansion to landowners' high rents and cheap cooperative financing through the Central Japonesa, calling for Banco Agricola reform and regulation of land leases and credit.

subfiles.title: La Infiltración Japonesa: Se siente en el ambiente la pauperización y desplazamiento de brazos que origina la inmigración japonesa
subfiles.doc_type: Newspaper clipping; Enclosure No. 39 to despatch No. 245
subfiles.about: A demand to halt Japanese immigration on the grounds that it displaced Peruvian labor and preserved a separate Japanese national identity.
subfiles.summary: Figueros claims Japanese firms evade labor laws, pay low wages and displace Peruvians; Japanese schools inculcate loyalty to Japan; alleges efforts to consolidate land at Tulumayo.

subfiles.title: La Infiltración Japonesa: Un punto sobre cada i—Nuevos conceptos sobre los mismos errores
subfiles.doc_type: Newspaper clipping; Enclosure No. 40 to despatch No. 245
subfiles.from: H. Ikeyama, Director of Perú Jiho
subfiles.to: Guillermo Salinas Cossío and La Prensa readers
subfiles.about: Ikeyama answers Salinas Cossío’s allegations concerning Japanese trade, agricultural activity, diplomacy, remittances, and population in Peru.
subfiles.summary: Ikeyama denies Japan's free trade is dumping, disputes the 60 percent export claim, credits immigrants with better cotton yields rather than fiber, and keeps an estimate of 23,000 immigrants.

subfiles.title: La Infiltración Japonesa: Esta discusión no es de figuras literarias, sino de vida o muerte para el Perú
subfiles.doc_type: Newspaper clipping; Enclosure No. 41 to despatch No. 245
subfiles.to: H. Ikeyama and La Prensa readers
subfiles.about: A rebuttal to Ikeyama assembling claims that Japanese residents were gaining control of land, commerce, transportation, and institutions in Peru.
subfiles.summary: Zegarra cites correspondents to argue Japanese networks excluded Peruvians from farming, commerce and transport, and that Japanese schools, press and high birth rates threaten Peruvian nationality; urges enforcement of quotas and surveillance.

subfiles.title: La Inmigración Asiática en el Perú
subfiles.doc_type: Newspaper clipping; Enclosure No. 42 to despatch No. 245
subfiles.from: Semana, reporting an interview with Rivera Schreiber
subfiles.about: A brief report on Peruvian enforcement of immigration law against passengers arriving from the Far East.
subfiles.summary: Rivera Schreiber says a Foreign Relations commission inspects each vessel from the Far East; few Japanese or Chinese are admitted and several travelers were returned at the shipping company's expense.

subfiles.title: El Peligro Amarillo en América: El Japón pretende absorber nuestras industrias y comercio—La democracia de América en peligro
subfiles.doc_type: Newspaper clipping; Enclosure No. 43 to despatch No. 245
subfiles.about: An alarmist article portraying Japanese migration, commerce, and alleged espionage as part of an imperial plan for domination of the Pacific and South America.
subfiles.summary: 'The Yellow Peril in America': Japan seeks Pacific control and espionage networks in the US and Panama, with Peru the first likely victim; relies on racial hierarchy; 'to be continued'.

subfiles.title: El Chisme del Día: Filantropía Asiática
subfiles.doc_type: Satirical newspaper column; Enclosure No. 44 to despatch No. 245
subfiles.about: A sarcastic attack on Ikeyama’s claim that Japanese enterprises such as Perú Takushoku Kumiai advanced Peru’s prosperity without seeking profit.
subfiles.summary: Satirical column calls Japanese activity 'philanthropy' while alleging displacement of Peruvian tenants and workers, violation of labor-percentage laws and bribery in the Chancay Valley.

subfiles.title: La Infiltración Japonesa: Desde el Comercio Minorista Hasta las Empresas Colonizadoras de la Montaña
subfiles.doc_type: Newspaper clipping; Enclosure No. 45 to despatch No. 245
subfiles.from: H. Ikeyama, Director of Perú Jiho
subfiles.to: Guillermo Salinas Cossío and La Prensa readers
subfiles.about: Ikeyama defends Japanese participation in urban trades and explains the cooperative agricultural settlement established by Perú Takushoku Kumiai in Chanchamayo.
subfiles.summary: Ikeyama says Japanese merchants mostly bought businesses from Chinese and Italians, disputes bakery figures, and describes Peru Takushoku Kumiai's nonprofit coffee-and-maize colony in Chanchamayo.
